tagline: A former Mississippi port and an inland battlefield mark Grant’s campaign.
intro: Grand Gulf’s riverfront history now belongs to a ghost town: the Mississippi shifted west and left the former port landlocked. At the other end of the journey, Raymond occupies a ridge chosen for the county seat because lower ground was subject to flooding.

In April 1863, Confederate defenses at Grand Gulf withstood a Union naval bombardment, so Ulysses S. Grant crossed the Mississippi farther south at Bruinsburg. Victory at Port Gibson forced the Confederates to abandon Grand Gulf, which became a Union supply point. After the Battle of Raymond, Grant turned toward Confederate forces at Jackson before advancing on Vicksburg.

Begin with the surviving Fort Wade and Fort Cobun earthworks at Grand Gulf. Rocky Springs, between Old Port Gibson Road and the Natchez Trace Parkway, preserves remnants of a former watering place. Finish in Raymond, where the courthouse and water tower are town landmarks.

moments.title: Grand Gulf
moments.text: Grand Gulf took its name from a whirlpool formed where the Mississippi struck a rocky bluff. Cotton from three counties passed through its wharves, and a railroad connected the port with inland Port Gibson. Union forces burned the town during the Civil War. Afterward, the river shifted west and left it landlocked as the population continued to decline. The military state park preserves Fort Wade and Fort Cobun earthworks, with a museum and interpretive exhibits documenting the battle. By 1900, its population had fallen to 150, following the decline after the Civil War.

moments.title: Rocky Springs
moments.text: A post office safe and a cistern survive along Rocky Springs’ short loop trail. The settlement began in the late 1700s as a watering place on the old Natchez Trace, taking its name from a spring and rock outcrop. Its decline began during the Civil War; later came yellow fever, boll weevils and severe soil erosion. The last store closed in 1930, and the spring dried up. The Methodist church built in 1837 is the only remaining building; regular Sunday services ended in 2010 as the congregation dwindled. National Park Service placards explain the town’s growth and decline along the trail.
moments.notice: A post office safe and a cistern remain along the short loop trail.

moments.title: Raymond
moments.text: Raymond’s courthouse took shape between 1857 and 1859, built largely by enslaved African Americans. After the Battle of Raymond on May 12, 1863, the building served as a Confederate field hospital while Union wounded were treated in local churches. Union soldiers used St. Mark’s Episcopal Church as a hospital. The courthouse remains in use for county legal matters, with Jackson serving as the primary county seat. A water tower begun in 1903 shares the town square with it. The Friends of Raymond provides public interpretation of part of the nearby battlefield.
